full_title: LILY C. LOPEZ, PETITIONER, VS. LOLITO S. LOPEZ, MA. RACHEL NICOLETTE LOPEZ, BARBARA VILLAS, BENEDICTO VILLAFUERTE, MA. LUISA PARAS, RUEL VILLACORTA, TERESITA C. FERNANDO, AND i SPECIALIST DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION, RESPONDENTS. LOLITO S. LOPEZ, MARIO S. LOPEZ, ANDRESITO S. LOPEZ, BARBARA O. VILLAS, BENEDICTO L. VILLAFUERTE, MA. LUISA I. PARAS, RUEL S. VILLACORTA, TERESITA C. FERNANDO, LC LOPEZ RESOURCES, INC., AND CONQUEROR INTERNATIONAL, INC., RESPONDENTS.
subject: Commercial and Taxation Laws
syllabus_topic: I. Business Organizations > A. Corporations (RA 11232) > 6. Directors and Trustees > a. Repository of Corporate Powers
topics: Sale of unissued shares requires a board resolution; invalidly acquired shares cannot be voted
Proof of stockholder status: stock and transfer book vs. GIS and other evidence; estoppel
Quorum in a special stockholders' meeting
Presumption of regularity of a court certification of receipt; late petition for review in an intra-corporate case

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > c. Perfection of Appeal

doctrine:
**Corporate powers are exercised, all business conducted, and all corporate property controlled by the board of directors** (Section 23, Corporation Code). A corporate president, even one who is a majority stockholder, cannot validly buy the corporation's unissued shares without a board resolution authorizing the sale. **The sale is invalid, and the shares cannot be voted** in electing directors. A sale of unissued shares made without first offering them to the other stockholders also violates their **preemptive right** (Section 39, Corporation Code). A stockholders' meeting where the shares represented are less than one-half plus one of the outstanding shares lacks a quorum and is void, together with the election held at it.

The stock and transfer book (STB) generally controls who are stockholders (Lao v. Lao; F & S Velasco v. Madrid). That rule does not apply squarely where stockholder status is proved by evidence other than the General Information Sheet (GIS), such as admissions of the adverse party and notices of meeting sent to the person as a stockholder. A party who presented a person as a stockholder in his dealings with banks is **estopped** from denying that status. Where the STB entries are of doubtful veracity, the latest GIS may be used to determine the outstanding shares for quorum purposes.

On procedure, a branch clerk of court's certification that counsel, through a messenger, received the decision on a stated date enjoys the **presumption of regularity**, which only clear and convincing evidence can overcome; the burden is on the party disputing receipt. A petition for review filed beyond the 15-day period under A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC must be dismissed, because perfecting an appeal within the period is jurisdictional. (Rules reiterated and applied.)
facts:
Spouses Lily and Lolito Lopez owned the majority shares of i Specialist Development Corporation (i Specialist), which they had run since 2011 with Lolito as president. They were also stockholders of the family corporations LC Lopez Resources, Inc. (LC Lopez) and Conqueror International, Inc. (Conqueror). Without any board resolution authorizing the sale, Lolito bought unissued shares of these corporations: 33,495 unissued shares of i Specialist, whose 2013 GIS showed only 12,500 common shares (5,592 each for the spouses), and, on November 26, 2018, 252,125 unissued shares of LC Lopez and 97,050 of Conqueror. He used these shares to elect new boards.

*Quezon City case.* On February 14, 2019, Lolito, as president, held a special stockholders' meeting of i Specialist at a restaurant in Quezon City, where a new board was elected. Lily and her daughter Christina sued in the RTC of Quezon City, Branch 93, a special commercial court. On July 29, 2019, the RTC declared the meeting and election void ab initio. Lolito had admitted that no board resolution authorized his purchase, so the shares could not be voted, and they were numerous enough to affect the election.

*Marikina case.* At the February 11, 2019 special stockholders' meeting of LC Lopez and Conqueror, the proxies of the couple's children Christina and John Rusty were turned away on the ground that the children were not stockholders. Lily walked out after her lawyer was not allowed to stay, and a new board was elected. The children were listed as stockholders in the GIS but not in the STB. The STB entries, and the stock certificates of Lolito and his co-defendants, had been made only days before the meeting by the accounting head, Edna Victoria, not by the corporate secretary, and the corporate secretary did not know what documents supported them. Lolito and two co-defendants confirmed that the children were stockholders, Lolito had sent them notices of the meeting, and he had recognized them as directors in bank transactions. Under the 2017 GIS, LC Lopez had 162,500 outstanding shares and Conqueror 45,000; only Lolito's 61,750 and 17,100 shares, respectively, were represented. On September 13, 2019, the RTC of Marikina, Branch 273 declared the meeting and the election void. It found the children to be stockholders, held that there was no quorum, nullified Lolito's share purchases (no board resolution and violation of Lily's preemptive right), and held Lolito estopped.

On petitions for review, the CA, in a consolidated Decision dated February 26, 2020, reversed both RTCs and declared the meetings valid. It held the Quezon City petition timely. The RTC-QC branch clerk had certified that respondents' counsel, through a certain Richard Belasco, personally received the decision on August 6, 2019, which would make the August 28, 2019 filing late under the 15-day period of A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC. The CA discounted the certification because there was no proof that Belasco was authorized to receive the decision. It also ruled that Christina was not a stockholder because she was not in the STB, and that Lolito's purchase was merely an ultra vires act, justified by the need for capital and capable of ratification by the board.
issues: Whether respondents' petition for review in CA-G.R. SP No. 162134 (the Quezon City case) was timely filed.
Whether Christina is a stockholder of the subject corporations.
Whether Lolito's purchase of the unissued shares was valid, and whether the special stockholders' meetings were valid.
ruling:
**1. No, it was filed late.** The certification that counsel, through Belasco, personally received the decision on August 6, 2019 was issued by an officer of the court and carries the presumption of regularity. Before that date, the parties had been told in open court that the decision would be promulgated on or about July 30, 2019, and the judge had encouraged them to get their copies personally. With the presumption in petitioner's favor, the burden shifted to respondents to prove, for example, that Belasco was not an employee of their law firm or was not authorized to receive the decision. They did not; their counsel only asked the court whether the firm had sent any letter authorizing him. **The presumption can be overthrown only by clear and convincing evidence** (Yap v. Lagtapon), and the CA erred in requiring petitioner to prove Belasco's authority. Because perfecting an appeal within the reglementary period is jurisdictional (Building Care Corp. v. Macaraeg), the Court held that respondents' petition in CA-G.R. SP No. 162134 must be dismissed on this procedural ground alone, without ruling on its merits, leaving the RTC-QC decision standing.

**2. Yes, Christina is a stockholder.** Lao does not squarely apply because Christina proved her status by evidence other than the GIS. Lolito, Villafuerte and Fernando all confirmed in their testimonies that Christina and John Rusty were stockholders, and Lolito even sent the two notices of the special meeting. **Having presented Christina as a stockholder in his dealings with banks, Lolito is estopped from denying that status** when doing so would serve his interests.

**3. No, the purchase was invalid, and the meetings were void.** Under Section 23 of the Corporation Code, corporate powers are exercised by the board. **Without a board resolution authorizing the sale of the unissued shares, Lolito could not validly buy them, and he could not legally use them to vote for a new set of directors.** The sale also violated petitioner's preemptive right under Section 39. In addition, the special stockholders' meeting was void for lack of quorum. Because the STB entries were of doubtful veracity (made by Edna, who was not the corporate secretary, a few days before the meeting, apparently without supporting documents), the Court used the latest GIS. Only Lolito's 61,750 of LC Lopez's 162,500 outstanding shares, and only his shares out of Conqueror's 45,000, were represented, because the other stockholders and their proxies were prevented from attending. His shares alone could not make up "the one-half plus one of the total outstanding shares required to have a quorum." **The special stockholders' meeting and the sale and voting of the unissued shares were void and produced no legal effect.**
disposition: The petition was GRANTED. The CA Decision in CA-G.R. SP Nos. 162134 and 162787 was SET ASIDE. The Decisions of the RTC of Quezon City, Branch 93 (voiding the February 14, 2019 special stockholders' meeting and election of i Specialist) and of the RTC of Marikina City, Branch 273 (voiding the February 11, 2019 special stockholders' meeting of LC Lopez and Conqueror and the election held there) were REINSTATED in toto.

bar_questions.q: Ramon is the president of Alpha Corp. and owns 45% of its outstanding shares; his estranged wife Sonia owns another 45%. Without any board resolution, Ramon paid for 30,000 of Alpha's unissued shares and had himself recorded as their owner. He never offered any of these shares to Sonia or the other stockholders, and the articles of incorporation do not deny preemptive rights. At a special stockholders' meeting, Ramon voted his original and newly acquired shares to elect a new board that excluded Sonia. Sonia sued to nullify the election. Ramon argues that he acted to infuse urgently needed capital and that the purchase was at most an ultra vires act that the board may ratify. Is the election valid?

alac.answer: No. Ramon's purchase of the unissued shares is invalid, so the shares could not be voted, and the election they carried is void.
alac.legal_basis: Corporate powers are exercised, all business conducted, and all corporate property controlled by the board of directors (Section 23, Corporation Code; now Section 22, Revised Corporation Code). Without a board resolution authorizing the sale of unissued shares, a corporate officer cannot validly purchase them, and shares so acquired cannot be voted in electing directors. A sale made without first offering the shares to the other stockholders also violates their preemptive right (Section 39, Corporation Code; now Section 38, Revised Corporation Code). (Lopez v. Lopez, G.R. Nos. 254957-58, June 15, 2022)
alac.application: The sale of unissued shares is a corporate act that only Alpha's board can authorize. Ramon, though president and a major stockholder, acted without any board resolution, so the sale is invalid. His reasons, the need for capital and the possibility of ratification, do not supply the missing board authority; the Court rejected the same arguments in Lopez. The sale also bypassed Sonia's preemptive right, because the shares were not first offered to existing stockholders in proportion to their holdings. Since the 30,000 shares were invalidly acquired, they could not be voted, and an election decided by them is void.
alac.conclusion: The election is void because it was carried by unissued shares sold without board authority and in violation of Sonia's preemptive right.

bar_questions.q: Beta Corp. is a family corporation. Its latest General Information Sheet lists the father (40%), the mother (40%) and their two children (10% each) as stockholders. The stock and transfer book shows only the father; its entries were written by the company accountant, not the corporate secretary, a week before a special stockholders' meeting, with no supporting documents. The father sent the children notices of the meeting as stockholders and had earlier presented them to banks as stockholders and directors. At the meeting, the children's proxies were turned away, the mother walked out, and only the father's shares were represented when a new board was elected. (a) May the father deny that the children are stockholders because they are not in the stock and transfer book? (b) Was there a quorum?

alac.answer: (a) No. The children proved their status by evidence other than the GIS, and the father is estopped from denying it. (b) No. Only 40% of the outstanding shares was represented, so the meeting and the election are void.
alac.legal_basis: The rule that the stock and transfer book, not the GIS, controls stockholder status (Lao v. Lao) does not apply squarely where status is proved by other evidence, such as the adverse party's admissions and notices of meeting sent to the person as a stockholder. One who held out a person as a stockholder in bank transactions is estopped from denying that status when it would prejudice his interests. Where the STB entries are of doubtful veracity, the latest GIS may be used to determine whether a quorum, one-half plus one of the outstanding shares, was present. (Lopez v. Lopez, G.R. Nos. 254957-58, June 15, 2022)
alac.application: The children's status rests not only on the GIS but on the father's own notices to them as stockholders and his representation to banks that they were stockholders and directors. He cannot now disown that status to suit his interest. The STB is unreliable because its entries were made by someone other than the corporate secretary, days before the meeting, without supporting documents. Using the GIS, the father's 40% falls short of the majority of outstanding shares needed for a quorum.
alac.conclusion: The children are stockholders, and the special meeting and the election held at it are void for lack of quorum.

bar_questions.q: In an intra-corporate election contest, the RTC, acting as a special commercial court, ruled against the newly elected directors of XYZ Corp. The branch clerk of court certified that the directors' counsel, through a messenger named Paolo, personally received a copy of the decision on March 3, 2025. The directors filed a petition for review with the Court of Appeals on March 25, 2025. They argue that the certification deserves no weight because the winning party never proved that Paolo worked for their law firm or was authorized to receive the decision. Their only evidence is that their counsel asked the court whether any letter from the firm had authorized Paolo, and was told there was none. Should the Court of Appeals give due course to the petition?

alac.answer: No. The petition was filed beyond the 15-day period and must be dismissed.
alac.legal_basis: A certification by an officer of the court that counsel received a copy of a decision carries the presumption of regularity in the performance of official duties, which only clear and convincing evidence can overthrow. The burden is on the party disputing receipt, not on the party relying on the certification. Under A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC, a decision in an intra-corporate controversy is reviewed by petition for review filed within 15 days, and perfecting an appeal within the reglementary period is jurisdictional; failure to do so makes the judgment final and executory. (Lopez v. Lopez, G.R. Nos. 254957-58, June 15, 2022, citing Yap v. Lagtapon and Building Care Corp. v. Macaraeg)
alac.application: The clerk's certification is presumed regular, so it was the directors, not the winning party, who had to prove that Paolo was not their employee or was not authorized. The absence of an authorization letter on file falls far short of clear and convincing evidence. Counted from March 3, 2025, the 15-day period ended on March 18, 2025, so the March 25 filing was late. The RTC decision became final and executory.
alac.conclusion: The Court of Appeals should dismiss the petition for review for having been filed out of time.

notes: The decision cites Sections 23 and 39 of the Corporation Code (B.P. Blg. 68), quoting the old Section 23. Footnote 73 quotes the preemptive-right provision under the heading "Section 38." The Revised Corporation Code (R.A. No. 11232) counterparts are Section 22 (board of directors) and Section 38 (preemptive right); the Court did not discuss the RCC. The source text has minor inconsistencies. The facts say respondents' counsel checked with the RTC on "02 October 2022," a date after the decision itself. The quorum discussion gives Lolito's Conqueror shares as "17,000," while the GIS figures quoted earlier give 17,100. The Court's ruling speaks only of Christina's status, although the Marikina RTC also found John Rusty to be a stockholder.
